title: How RNAscope works
objective: Explain how double-Z probes make RNAscope specific and amplified.

steps.title: Two probes must agree
steps.body: **[[RNAscope]]** uses pairs of **double-Z (ZZ) probes**. The preamplifier only binds when *two* adjacent Z probes land side by side on the mRNA. A single probe sticking non-specifically can't build signal — it takes two neighbors to start the tree. That double requirement is what makes it specific.

visual.alt: An mRNA tiled by ZZ probe pairs (three shown, more continue). A preamplifier binds across each pair's two side-by-side Z tails, amplifiers branch off it, and label probes light up so the trees merge into one bright dot. A lone probe stuck on an off-target strand has no partner, so nothing binds it and it stays dark, marked with a cross.
visual.caption: Only two Z probes side by side can start the tree, so a lone stray probe stays dark.

steps.prompt: Order how an RNAscope signal is built.
items: A pair of ZZ probes binds adjacent sites on the target mRNA
A preamplifier binds across the two Z tails
Each mRNA appears as a bright dot
steps.explanation: The paired-probe requirement gates the whole cascade; the tree then amplifies one transcript into a visible dot.

steps.prompt: Why does requiring *two* adjacent probes cut background?
options: A single off-target probe cannot trigger amplification alone
Two adjacent probes simply bind the target faster than one
It roughly doubles the brightness of each fluorophore used
Each probe can be half as long, so it mismatches less often
steps.explanation: Non-specific binding is usually a lone probe. With no adjacent partner, no amplifier assembles — so stray binding stays dark.

variants.setup: One ZZ probe sticks somewhere off-target, with no partner nearby.
options: No — amplification needs both probes of the adjacent pair
Yes, it lights up as a bright but completely false dot
Yes, but as a dimmer dot than a true paired site
variants.reveal: The amplifier needs both Z tails side by side, so a lone off-target probe stays dark.

steps.title: One dot ≈ one transcript
steps.body: A probe set tiles each mRNA with ~20 ZZ pairs, and their trees pile up into one bright spot. So RNAscope is near single-molecule: individual mRNA copies show up as countable dots. That makes it quantitative *and* spatial — you can count transcripts per cell.

flag.note: Dot counts approximate transcript number; dense or overlapping signals need careful imaging and thresholds.

steps.prompt: Label the parts of the RNAscope signal tree.
steps.explanation: A ZZ probe pair lands on the mRNA, the preamplifier binds across its two tails, amplifiers branch off the preamplifier, and label probes carry the dye.

sources.citation: Wang F et al., 2012, J Mol Diagn
sources.note: Original RNAscope method: double-Z probes and tree amplification.

reviewNotes: RNAscope mechanism; the ZZ specificity trick.
